jj: I tried it so you do not have to

The problem it solves

Git is powerful, and it is also full of rough edges: the staging area, detached HEADs, interactive rebases that go wrong, work you lose because you forgot to stash. Jujutsu, jj, promises the same power with fewer ways to hurt yourself.

The general idea

jj is a version control system that stores its data in a normal Git repository, so it can work with GitHub and with colleagues who use git. It changes the model. There is no staging area: the working copy is itself a commit that is amended as you edit. Every change has a stable change ID that survives rewriting, history editing is a normal operation, and an operation log lets you undo almost anything, including a botched rebase.

Examples

jj git init --colocate     # use jj inside an existing git repo
jj new -m "try a new idea" # start a new change
jj log                     # the graph, with change ids
jj undo                    # rewind the last operation
jj git push                # publish a bookmark to the git remote

Tips from my setup

  • I tried it for real. I made a playground repository, learned the vocabulary (changes, bookmarks, the operation log) and wrote a just jj push recipe in my dotfiles: it fetches, lets me pick a bookmark with a fuzzy finder, previews the revisions to publish and pushes.
  • What I liked. No staging, an always-safe working copy and a real undo. Rewriting history feels natural instead of dangerous.
  • Why I went back to git. It is not compatible with DVC. DVC expects a git repository: it tracks its metadata in git, and experiments are built on git state. In my try the two did not work together, and since DVC is central to my pipelines, git stays. See the posts about git and DVC.
  • If you do not use DVC, give it a try. It is a good idea, and it works on top of the git you already have.
